title: Enterprise AI Agentic Management Platform
oneLiner: A modular React 19 frontend for managing AI agents, with role-based access and real-time analytics.

problem: The client needed one place to build, configure and run AI agents. The platform was organised into modules, such as Models, Solutions and Agents, each its own area of the app.
All four modules needed the same UI building blocks, the same access rules and live operational data, and building each one separately would have meant four slightly different products.
constraints: One component architecture had to serve four platform modules without forking.
Access control had to mean the same thing in frontend routing and in API-level authorization.
Identity came from Azure MSAL with OAuth 2.0.
A frontend team of four, so shared foundations mattered more than per-module polish.

decisions.title: A modular component architecture shared by four modules
decisions.body: I designed the component layer as composable primitives and module-level compositions, so each platform module consumed the same pieces instead of rebuilding them.

decisions.title: One role model, enforced in two places
decisions.body: I implemented RBAC on Azure MSAL and OAuth 2.0 with a single role model. The frontend used it to gate routes and UI, and the same roles drove API-level authorization, so the two could not drift apart.

decisions.title: Shaping the API contracts
decisions.body: I worked with the backend on the REST contracts the dashboards needed, and centralized data fetching and error handling in one Axios layer instead of per-component calls.

decisions.title: Cutting the bundle
decisions.body: I used code splitting, memoization and lazy loading to cut the bundle by about 30%, which took the Lighthouse performance score from 62 to 88.

decisions.title: GenAI-assisted delivery
decisions.body: I used GitHub Copilot heavily throughout the build for code generation, which sped up component and feature delivery while I kept ownership of the architecture and reviews.

result: Four platform modules shared one component architecture and one role model.

title: SaaS E-Learning & Publication Platform
oneLiner: A multi-tenant LMS split into independently deployable micro-frontends, with Node.js and PostgreSQL APIs on AWS.
ownership: Full-stack features across client and server

problem: Education companies needed to put learning resources in front of students and educators through accessible digital experiences. The platform supported back-to-school activities: helping people discover resources, understand how to access learning materials and get ready for the academic year.
Each education company ran as its own tenant, and the course, exam and admin experiences had to ship on their own schedules without one breaking the others.
constraints: Course, Exam and Admin had to be independently deployable.
Peak exam periods brought 10K+ concurrent users, so frontend failures had to be caught quickly.
A 21-person team working across the modules at once, so boundaries between them had to be clear.

decisions.title: Micro-frontends with Module Federation
decisions.body: I architected the LMS as a host with Course, Exam and Admin remotes using Webpack Module Federation, so each module could build and deploy independently. Teams could work in parallel, and a failure in one module stayed in that module.

decisions.title: Full-stack LMS features
decisions.body: I built course management, exam workflows and student performance tracking end to end: React, TypeScript, Redux Toolkit and React Router v6 on the client, and Node.js, Express and PostgreSQL on the server.

decisions.title: REST APIs on AWS
decisions.body: I built REST APIs with Node.js and Express on AWS EC2, backed by PostgreSQL, with S3 for static assets and CloudWatch for monitoring. That cut frontend mean time to detect issues by 40% during peak exam periods with 10K+ concurrent users.

decisions.title: Admin dashboards
decisions.body: I built the admin dashboards with Ant Design and Styled-Components, wired to the REST APIs through Axios for real-time data and reporting. Admin screens are mostly dense tables, forms, filters and date pickers, and Ant Design ships all of those with accessibility and keyboard support built in. That let me spend the time on admin workflows instead of building primitives, while Styled-Components kept the theme consistent with the rest of the platform.

decisions.title: Standards that scale the team
decisions.body: I set up a shared component library and PR review standards, which made onboarding faster and lowered the UI bug rate.

result: Frontend MTTD dropped by 40% during peak exam periods with 10K+ concurrent users.
Course, Exam and Admin deployed independently, and teams developed them in parallel.
Onboarding got faster and the UI bug rate went down after the shared library and review standards.

title: EdTech Learning Platform
oneLiner: A course platform where learners pay to enroll and learn: React and Next.js on the client, Node.js on AWS Lambda behind API Gateway, and Stripe billing.

problem: An online course platform: learners browse a catalogue, pay to enroll in courses and learn at their own pace, while instructors create and manage their courses.
It needed student dashboards, instructor portals and course workflows, with payments and recurring billing that worked without manual chasing.
constraints: A 4-person agile team, so everyone worked across the stack.
Serverless AWS: Lambda, API Gateway and DynamoDB.
Recurring billing and invoicing had to run without manual chasing.

decisions.title: End-to-end product features
decisions.body: I built student dashboards, instructor portals and course workflows end to end: React, Next.js and TypeScript on the client, and Node.js on the server.

decisions.title: Serverless APIs
decisions.body: I wrote Node.js Lambda functions and REST APIs exposed through API Gateway, with DynamoDB for persistence, so the backend scaled without servers to manage.

decisions.title: Webhook-driven billing
decisions.body: I integrated Stripe with webhook event handling for recurring subscription billing and automated invoicing, so payment state changes reached the app as they happened. Failed payment follow-ups dropped by 60%.

result: The MVP shipped two weeks ahead of schedule.
There were zero critical post-launch defects.

title: PBI AutoBuilder
oneLiner: From raw data and a client brief to a ready-to-open Power BI dashboard: a React + Node.js app that generates the cleaning, model, DAX and report for you.
ownership: Solo project: design, frontend, backend and Power BI generation

problem: Building a Power BI dashboard from raw data repeats the same steps on every project: understanding the business, cleaning messy data in Power Query, designing a data model, writing DAX measures and laying out visuals.
Analysts spend hours clicking through the same transformations, and beginners often get the model or the DAX wrong.
constraints: Data had to stay private: it was designed to run locally, and the AI receives only schema statistics and about 15 sample rows, never the full dataset.
It had to produce reliable output with free or small AI models, and with no AI at all.
The exported project had to refresh on any PC, with no file paths to fix.
What the user previews had to match exactly what Power BI loads.

howItWorks.title: Upload
howItWorks.body: Raw CSV or Excel data, plus the client brief.

howItWorks.title: Understand
howItWorks.body: Profiles every column (types, blanks, duplicates, inconsistent casing, currency symbols, mixed date formats) and summarises the business, the questions to answer and the KPIs.

howItWorks.title: Clean
howItWorks.body: Suggests Power Query steps from a library of 18 operations, such as type fixes, trimming, replacing values, de-duplication, splitting columns, calculated columns, and bands like DPD buckets and age groups. A live before/after preview and the generated M code sit side by side.

howItWorks.title: Model
howItWorks.body: Designs a star schema, detecting fact and dimension tables from key uniqueness, including one-to-one keys shared across several sources. Generates a Date table marked as the date table, shown as an interactive diagram.

howItWorks.title: Measures
howItWorks.body: Writes layered DAX: base measures, then ratios with DIVIDE, then time intelligence (YTD, PY, YoY, MoM). A built-in linter checks every table and column reference.

howItWorks.title: Dashboard
howItWorks.body: Lays out KPI cards, trend and breakdown charts, a matrix and slicers on an automatic grid, with a colour theme. A live preview computes the real numbers.

howItWorks.title: Export
howItWorks.body: Generates a Power BI Project (.pbip) with a TMDL semantic model, a PBIR report and a theme, plus a README documenting every cleaning step and measure, the expected totals and demo talking points.

decisions.title: The AI decides, templates generate
decisions.body: The language model never writes Power BI files. It returns small JSON specs (cleaning operations, schema, measures, visual list) that are validated with zod, shown to the user and turned into Power Query M, TMDL and PBIR by tested generators. A deterministic rules engine produces every step with no AI at all.

decisions.title: One engine, two outputs
decisions.body: Every cleaning operation is implemented twice, as JavaScript for the live preview and as Power Query M for Power BI, so what the user previews is what Power BI loads.

decisions.title: A small DAX evaluator
decisions.body: It computes measures (SUM, COUNT, DISTINCTCOUNT, DIVIDE, CALCULATE with filters) directly from the data. That powers the dashboard preview and gives the user expected totals to check after refresh.

decisions.title: Portable output
decisions.body: The raw data is compressed (deflate + base64) inside the Power Query step, like Power BI’s “Enter data”, so the exported project refreshes on any PC without file paths.

decisions.title: Domain-aware rules
decisions.body: The engine recognises patterns such as days-past-due columns, credit scores and dates of birth, and generates collections KPIs (Delinquency %, NPA %, Overdue Outstanding) and analysis bands from them.

decisions.title: Private and provider-agnostic AI
decisions.body: It can run entirely on your own machine and work offline through Ollama, and a hosted version is available to try. Any OpenAI-compatible model (Google Gemini, Groq, OpenRouter, Ollama) can be switched from the Settings page.

result: A 7-step wizard that exports a Power BI Project which opens in Power BI Desktop.
About 8,000 lines of TypeScript: about 4,700 for the server, 2,900 for the client and 330 of shared types.
Unit tests (Vitest) cover value parsing, M generation, the DAX linter and evaluator, Excel date handling and the embedded-data round trip.

Tested end to end on a deliberately messy retail export (1,844 rows with mixed date formats, currency text, duplicates and blank rows) and a 3-table banking collections dataset (3,000 rows across loans, customers and bureau data).
learned: How Power BI stores reports and models as text (TMDL, PBIR), and how Power Query and DAX evaluate data.
How to design LLM features so they’re reliable: structured output, schema validation and a deterministic fallback.
How to debug real-world issues once a project leaves my own PC, such as file paths and zip extraction on another computer.
